title: Rethinking the Screen: A Case for Intention Over Elimination
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Responding to news of parents opting children out of school-issued Chromebooks, Marcinek argues the school-screens debate has become too binary. He agrees that devices are often used as pacifiers and that schools have over-relied on them, but he rejects calls to eliminate edtech, citing a Stanford-led meta-analysis showing positive but highly variable effects on early literacy and workforce data on digital literacy demand. His diagnosis is that digital literacy was treated as a separate subject rather than a skill, and that teachers were handed devices without sustained professional learning. He offers school leaders three low-cost steps: audit one lesson per grade for intentionality, replace one-off tech PD with embedded peer coaching, and publish a one-page screen-use framework for families. The thesis is that the answer is accountability and intention, not removal.
points: The real question is not whether edtech works but under what conditions, since the research shows wide variability tied to implementation.
Removing screens does not solve the digital-literacy gap; it delays it, and likely costs lower-income students most.
Computer-lab 'technology class' taught the skill in isolation from where it is applied, so it never transferred.
One-time tech workshops do not move the needle; sustained, embedded, contextual professional learning does.
Leaders can start by asking teachers to write one sentence justifying why a device is used in a given lesson.
quotes: That’s exactly why I pushed back when I saw voices in this debate calling for the elimination of edtech altogether. The frustration is understandable. The conclusion isn’t. There’s a significant distance between “screens are being misused in schools” — which is true — and “remove them forever” — which doesn’t hold up, and which I’d argue actually harms the kids it’s trying to protect.

A Stanford-led meta-analysis of 119 studies published between 2010 and 2023 found that edtech produces positive effects on early literacy — with wide variability depending on implementation. That variability is the whole conversation. It’s not “does edtech work.” It’s “under what conditions does it work, and are we creating those conditions.

Here’s what I think is actually broken: we have treated digital literacy like a subject instead of a skill. For decades, “technology class” meant pulling kids out of their regular learning environment, sitting them in a computer lab for 45 minutes, and calling it integration. It wasn’t. It was isolation.

Research published in PMC is unambiguous: insufficient teacher preparation is one of the most significant barriers to effective technology use in schools. When training and ongoing support are provided, student outcomes improve. When they aren’t, you get Chromebooks used as digital hall passes.
What we did during and after the pandemic was hand teachers devices, wish them luck, and call it transformation. It wasn’t. It was abandonment dressed up as innovation.

The parents in that NBC article are responding to something real. Schools have over-relied on devices as a substitute for human instruction, and that’s not defensible. But the solution isn’t amputation. It’s accountability.
The solution isn’t less technology; it’s better technology. We don’t need removal, but intentional use.
